newsitem.title: BELGIUM: A single telecoms market still an elusive EU goal.
newsitem.headline: A single telecoms market still an elusive EU goal.

text.p: All European Union countries have made progress in opening their telecommunications markets to competition, but they are still far from forming a single market, telecoms experts said on Monday.

While Britain and Sweden earned top marks for compliance with the EU's liberalisation plan in a study by telecoms consultancy Yankee Group Europe, Greece scored only 2.2, Austria 2.6 and Portugal 2.9 out of a possible 5.

"This gives us some cause for concern about whether they will be able to achieve this objective (of a single market) in the future and how long it's going to take," the group's director, Graham Finnie, told reporters at a telecoms seminar.

He and officials from British Telecommunications Plc, which sponsored the seminar, also highlighted the need for continued regulatory vigilance as countries implement the EU plan for abolishing phone monopolies in most countries by January 1, 1998.

"Many more resources need to be put into implementation and enforcement of the 1998 measures," said Mike Corkerry, BT's head of regulatory affairs, adding that he welcomed the European Commission's decision to set up an internal task force to push liberalisation laggards.
Finnie noted that 54 percent of western Europe's $158 billion telecoms market was still controlled by monopolies -- the voice telephone sector that is due to be opened up in 1998.

While powerful rivals to the traditional phone companies are emerging across Europe, some regulatory questions still need to be resolved such as how to calculate the fees newcomers are charged to hook up to the former monopolies' networks, he said.
Without a clear position by an independent regulator, "the situation is bound to benefit the incumbent operator," he said.

Finnie complained that some existing EU laws have not been implemented properly -- such as one requiring tariffs for leased circuits to be based on actual costs. "The cost of leased circuits is far higher than it should be," he said.

He cited a range of problems in individual countries, including the absence of an independent regulatory body in Germany, and said the EU's liberalisation plan would benefit some customers more than others.
Even by 2001, suburban and rural residential customers are not likely to see much competition for local calls, he said.
Corkerry expressed concern about the plethora of telecoms regulatory bodies and committees in the EU, although said the time was not ripe politically for an EU-wide regulatory body.

Finnie said "equal access" systems allowing consumers to use long-distance services of competitors withou having to dial a special code -- a subject now under discussion by the EU -- would allow newcomers to gain market share more quickly.
